analysis.one_liner: Requires a background check through a licensed dealer for nearly all private firearm sales and transfers.
analysis.headline: The Background Check Expansion Act was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a committee vote, floor vote, or any further action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for a private person to sell or transfer a firearm to another private person unless a licensed gun dealer first takes possession of the gun and runs a background check on the buyer, the same check that already applies at gun stores. Family gifts and loans, transfers to estates, urgent self-defense handoffs, and supervised target shooting or hunting loans would be exempt. The bill states it does not create a national gun registry.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially those in communities affected by gun violence. Closing the private-sale loophole means that people prohibited from owning guns because of felony convictions, domestic violence misdemeanors, or other disqualifying records could no longer buy firearms from unlicensed sellers with no check.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any transfer between unlicensed private parties unless a licensed dealer, manufacturer, or importer first takes possession of the firearm to conduct a background check, closing the private-sale loophole that applies when neither party holds a federal firearms license [S2][S3].

Requires dealers handling a private-sale check to follow the same procedures used for retail sales, including disqualification of prohibited purchasers under the existing background check system [S3].

Exempts transfers between spouses, domestic partners, parents and children, siblings, aunts and uncles and their nieces and nephews, and grandparents and grandchildren, as well as inheritance transfers, urgent self-defense handoffs, Attorney General-approved transfers, and temporary transfers for supervised target shooting, hunting, or fishing, so the requirement falls on stranger-to-stranger sales rather than everyday family and recreational transfers [S3].
Includes a rule of interpretation stating that nothing in the act may be construed to authorize a national firearms registry, and takes effect 180 days after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private gun owners and buyers, who would have to find a licensed dealer, hand over the firearm, complete the check, and pay any transfer fee the dealer charges before completing a sale or transfer that falls outside the exemptions. Licensed dealers take on new handling duties; the gun trade adjusts to every sale running through the licensed channel.

drawbacks.text: Law-abiding owners face a real burden: even a routine sale between two people at a gun show or through a classified ad would require the seller to deliver the firearm to a dealer, wait for the check, and pay a transfer fee, and the exemptions do not cover sales between, for example, cousins' spouses or unrelated hunting partners who travel separately [S3].

The check requirement applies to private transfers even when the buyer is a person the seller knows well, so honest owners bear paperwork and fees aimed at a small subset of transfers; opponents of universal checks have long argued that people who buy guns illegally to commit crimes would not use the licensed channel anyway, so the burden lands mostly on people already willing to comply. (This is a good-faith objection about effectiveness, not something the bill text addresses.)

The exemptions draw bright lines that can be arbitrary in practice, for example allowing an unchecked loan to a niece but requiring a check for a neighbor, which creates legal uncertainty for ordinary owners about exactly which transfers are covered [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: every firearm sale would pass through the same check that applies at gun stores, which is the single most direct way to keep guns away from people with disqualifying records. The costs are real but modest for most owners: a dealer visit and a fee for private sales, and some genuine gray areas in the exemption list. The design is careful about family, inheritance, and hunting situations, and explicitly rules out a registry. On balance the burden falls on transactions currently outside the law's reach, which is the point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2021 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no committee vote and no floor action through the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the Background Check Expansion Act on March 2, 2021, joined by 45 cosponsors, including Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and 44 of the Senate's 48 Democrats, plus Independent Senator Bernie Sanders [S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, the standard first step for a gun bill in the Senate [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no committee markup, no vote in committee, no floor debate, and no vote of any kind before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, private gun sellers and buyers who would have had to route every transfer through a licensed dealer are better off, and no one else gained anything concrete. The more notable fact is what did not happen: a bill cosponsored by 46 senators, including the majority leader, was never even brought up in committee, so the outcome reflects the Senate's decision not to act rather than a defeat on the merits.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 supporters were Senate Democrats plus the chamber's one sponsoring Independent; none of the 50 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the bill never advanced to a vote where crossover positions could be recorded.

industries.note: Every private sale would have to run through a licensed dealer, creating a new paid transfer-processing business line for dealers. Their gain comes alongside the bill's public-safety goal, since they are the checkpoint the law requires.

industries.industry: Firearm manufacturers and the gun trade
industries.note: Manufacturers would keep selling through the licensed channel, which already requires checks, but a requirement that all sales go through checks could reduce purchases by buyers who currently avoid them. The industry's interest in preserving unchecked private sales runs against the bill's safety purpose, while its licensed retail channel is the mechanism the bill builds on.
Owners would bear new dealer visits and transfer fees for private sales outside the family and hunting exemptions. Their cost is the flip side of the public benefit the bill is designed to produce.
